## Abstract

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-papillomaviruses are near-ubiquitous skin commensals, yet whether they are transcriptionally active in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) is unsettled. We reanalyzed over 10,000 public human RNA sequencing libraries, typing human papillomavirus (HPV), scoring productive infection from late (L1) capsid transcripts, and modeling detection against depth and chemistry. Productive infection was common in warts (`r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% of libraries above a viral load threshold calibrated on them) and epidermodysplasia verruciformis. cSCC and actinic keratosis libraries, although sequenced almost `r nword(stats$neo_medreads / stats$ctrl_medreads)` times more deeply, reached it in only `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`%, with a median viral load more than `r nword(floor(log10(stats$ctrl_medrpm / stats$neo_medrpm)))` orders of magnitude lower; the two did not differ. A minority of lesions carried productive beta- or alpha-HPV infection. The transcribed types were largely disjoint from the skin DNA reservoir: of its `r rv("n_dna_present")` types, `r rv("n_dna_present_silent")` were productive in no RNA library. HPV signal instead concentrated in nonprimary material: cell-line and engineered libraries had `r nword(mean(c(stats$cl_or, stats$eng_or)))`-fold higher odds of positivity (*P* < 10⁻⁷), mostly integrated HPV16 and HPV18, whereas HPV was detected in 2–3% of primary tissue libraries. Cutaneous HPV is therefore productive in warts but present only at trace, transcriptionally inactive levels in healthy skin and carcinoma, which models of beta-HPV in skin cancer must explain.
